<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|beat|493|beat}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''beat<sup>1</sup>''' (bēt), ''v.''; pret. ''beat'', pp. ''beaten'', ''beat'', ppr. ''beating''.   [< ME. ''beten'', < AS. ''beátan'' (pret. ''beót'', pp. ''beáten'') = OHG. ''bōzan'', MHG. ''bōzen'' = Icel. ''bauta'', beat. The superficial resemblance to F. ''battre'', E. ''bat''<sup>1</sup>, ''batter''<sup>1</sup>, is accidental, but has perhaps influenced some of the meanings of ''beat''<sup>1</sup>. Hence ''beetle''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To strike repeatedly; lay repeated blows upon.
{{smaller block|H’as ''beat'' me twice, and ''beat'' me to a coward.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Humorous Lieutenant, ii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|The eagles of Mexitli shall ''beat'' the air no more.
{{right|''Whittier'', The Crisis.}}}}
'''2.''' To strike in order to produce a sound; sound by percussion: as, to ''beat'' a drum or a tambourine.
{{smaller block|<poem>Come, ''beat'' all the drums up,
And all the noble instruments of war.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Humorous Lieutenant, v. 5.}}}}
'''3.''' To play (a particular call or tattoo) upon the drum: as, to ''beat'' a charge; to ''beat'' a retreat. [The last phrase often means simply to retire or retreat.]
{{smaller block|The enemy was driven back all day, as we had been the day before, until finally he ''beat'' a precipitate retreat.
{{right|''U. S. Grant'', Personal Memoirs, I. 350.}}}}
'''4.''' To break, bruise, comminute, or pulverize by beating or pounding, as any hard substance.
{{smaller block|Thou shalt ''beat'' some of it very small. {{right|Ex. xxx. 36.}}}}
'''5.''' To extend by beating, as gold or other malleable substance, or to hammer into any form; forge.
{{smaller block|They did ''beat'' the gold into thin plates. {{right|Ex. xxxix. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|The hammer which smote the Saracens at Tours was at last successful in ''beating'' the Netherlands into Christianity. {{right|''Motley'', Dutch Republic, I. 21.}}}}

'''6.''' To separate by concussion; strike apart; remove by striking or threshing: with ''out.''
{{smaller block|So she . . . ''beat out'' that she had gleaned: and it was about an ephah of barley.{{right|Ruth ii. 17.}}}}

'''7.''' To mix by a striking or beating motion; whip into the desired condition: as, to ''beat'' or ''beat'' up eggs or batter.—'''8.''' To dash or strike against, as water or wind.
{{smaller block|<poem>Beyond this flood a frozen continent
Lies, dark and wild, ''beat'' with perpetual storm.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 588.}}}}

'''9.''' To strike with the feet in moving; tread upon.
{{smaller block|<poem>Pass awful gulfs and ''beat'' my painful way.</poem>
{{right|''Sir R. Blackmore.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Along the margin of the moonlight sea
We ''beat'' with thundering hoofs the level sand.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Prelude, x.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Amid the sound of steps that ''beat''
The murmuring walks like autumn rain.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', The Crowded Street.}}}}

'''10.''' To range (fields or woods) with loud blows or other noise in search of game.
{{smaller block|To ''beat'' the woods and rouse the bounding prey.
{{right|''Prior.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Together let us ''beat'' this simple field,
Try what the open, what the covert yield!</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Essay on Man, i. 9.}}}}

'''11.''' To overcome in battle, contest, or strife; vanquish or conquer: as, one ''beats'' another at play.
{{smaller block|Pyrrhus . . . ''beat'' the Carthaginians at sea.
{{right|''Arbuthnot.''}}}}

'''12.''' To surpass; excel; go beyond: as, he ''beats'' them all at swimming. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|Many ladies in Strasburg were beautiful, still}}

{{smaller block|They were ''beat'' all to sticks by the lovely Odille.
{{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, I. 239.}}}}
{{smaller block|There is something out of common here that ''beats'' anything that ever came in my way. {{right|''Dickens.''}}}}
'''13.''' To be too difficult for, whether intellectually or physically; baffle: as, it ''beats'' me to make it out. [Colloq.]—'''14.''' To harass; exercise severely; cudgel (one’s brains).
{{smaller block|<poem>Sirrah, lay by your foolish study there,
And ''beat'' your brains about your own affairs.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher and Rowley'', Maid in the Mill, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Why should any one . . . ''beat'' his head about the Latin grammar who does not intend to be a critic? {{right|''Locke.''}}}}
'''15.''' To exhaust: as, the long and toilsome journey quite ''beat'' him. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|They had been ''beaten'' out with the exposure and hardship. {{right|''R. H. Dana, Jr.'', Before the Mast, p. 365.}}}}
'''16.''' To flutter; flap: as, to ''beat'' the wings: said of a bird. See ''bate''<sup>1</sup>.—'''17.''' In medieval embroidery, to ornament with thin plates of gold or silver.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hur clothys weyth bestes and byrdes wer ''bete'',
All abowte for pryde.</poem>
{{right|Quoted in ''Rock’s'' Textile Fabrics.}}}}
{{smaller block|One coat for my lord’s body ''beat'' with gold.
{{right|''Dugdale'', Baronage.}}}}
'''18.''' In ''printing'': (''a'') To ink with beaters. (''b'') To impress by repeatedly striking with a mallet a proof-planer pressed against the paper: as, ''beat'' a proof of that form.—'''19.''' To obtain an unfair advantage of; defraud: as, to ''beat'' a hotel. [Slang, U. S.] {{smaller|—'''To beat a bargain.''' See ''bargain.''—'''To beat a parley,''' to notify the enemy by a drum or trumpet signal that conference is desired under a flag of truce.—'''To beat away,''' in ''mining'', to excavate: usually applied to hard ground.—'''To beat back,''' to compel to retire or return.—'''To beat cock-fighting.''' See ''cock-fighting.''—'''To beat down.''' (''a'') To break, destroy, or throw down by beating or battering, as a wall. (''b'') To press down or lay flat (grass, grain, etc.) by any prostrating action, as that of a violent wind, a current of water, or the passage of persons or animals. (''c'') To cause to lower (a price) by importunity or argument; sink or lessen the price or value of; make lower, as price or value.}}
{{smaller block|It [usury] ''beats down'' the price of land. {{right|''Bacon'', Usury.}}}}
{{smaller|(''d'') To depress or crush: as, to ''beat down'' opposition.—'''To beat into,''' to teach or instil by repetition of instruction.—'''To beat off,''' to repel or drive back.—'''To beat out.''' (''a'') To extend by hammering; hence, figuratively, to work out fully; amplify; expand.}}
{{smaller block|A man thinking on his legs is obliged to ''beat out'' his thought for his own sake, if not for the sake of his hearers.
{{right|''Cornhill Mag.''}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') To perform or execute, as a piece of music, by or as if by beats with the hands or feet.}}
{{smaller block|The child’s feet were busy ''beating out'' the tune.
{{right|''Cornhill Mag.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Perplext in faith, but pure in deeds,
At last he ''beat'' his music ''out.''</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, xcvi.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') To drive out or away.}}
{{smaller block|Intermediate varieties, from existing in lesser numbers than the forms which they connect, will generally be ''beaten out'' and exterminated during the course of further modification and improvement.
{{right|''Darwin'', Origin of Species, p. 266.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To beat the air,''' to fight to no purpose, or against no antagonist or opposition.}}
{{smaller block|I therefore so run, not as uncertainly; so fight I, not as one that ''beateth'' the air.{{right|1 Cor. ix. 26.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To beat the bounds.''' See ''bound''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To beat the dust,''' in the ''manège'': (''a'') To take in too little ground with the fore legs, as a horse. (''b'') To curvet too precipitately or too low, as a horse.—'''To beat the general,''' to sound the roll of the drum which calls the troops together.—'''To beat the tattoo,''' to sound the drum for evening roll-call, when all soldiers except those absent with permission are expected to be present in their quarters.—'''To beat the wind,''' to make a few flourishes in the air, and thus be entitled to all the advantages of a victor, as was done under the medieval system of trial by battle when the other combatant failed to appear.—'''To beat time,''' to measure or regulate time in music by the motion of the hand or foot.—'''To beat to a mummy.''' See ''mummy''.—'''To beat up.''' (''a'') To attack suddenly; alarm or disturb; hence, to come to or upon unexpectedly: as, ''to beat up'' an enemy’s quarters.}}
{{smaller block|A distant relation left him an estate in Ireland, where he had resided ever since, making occasional visits to the Continent and ''beating up'' his old quarters, but rarely coming to England.{{right|''Lawrence.''}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') To summon or bring together as by beat of drum: as, to ''beat up'' recruits. (''c'') In ''hunting'', to rouse and drive (game) by ranging.}}
{{smaller block|They ''beat up'' a little game peradventure.{{right|''Lamb'', Imperfect Sympathies.}}}}
{{smaller|(''d'') In ''engraving'', to remove (a dent or mark) from the face of a plate by striking the back with a punch while the face rests on a sheet of tin-foil on an anvil or a stake. In this way engravers can remove marks too deep to be obliterated by the scraper or burnisher.='''Syn. 1.''' To pound, bang, buffet, maul, drub, thump, thwack, baste, thrash, pommel.—'''11.''' ''Discomfit'', ''Rout'', etc. See ''defeat''.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To strike repeatedly; knock, as at a door.
{{smaller block|The men of the city . . . ''beat'' at the door. Judges xix. 22.}}
'''2.''' To move with pulsation; throb: as, the pulse ''beats''. {{smaller block|A thousand hearts ''beat'' happily.
{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, iii. 21.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>With unused thoughts and sweet
And hurrying hopes, his heart began to ''beat''.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 408.}}}}
'''3.''' To act, dash, or fall with force or violence, as a storm, flood, passion, etc.: as, the tempest ''beats'' against the house.
{{smaller block|And the sun ''beat'' upon the head of Jonah, that he fainted, and wished in himself to die.
{{right|Jonah iv. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|Rolling tempests vainly ''beat'' below.
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
{{smaller block|For the noon is coming on, and the sunbeams fiercely ''beat''.
{{right|''Bryant'', Damsel of Peru.}}}}
'''4.''' To be tossed so as to strike the ground violently or frequently.
{{smaller block|Floating corps lie ''beating'' on the shore.
{{right|''Addison.''}}}}
'''5.''' To give notice by beating a drum; also, to sound on being beaten, as a drum.
{{smaller block|<poem>But Linden saw another sight
When the drum ''beat'' at dead of night.</poem>
{{right|''Campbell'', Hohenlinden.}}}}
'''6.''' To contain beats or pulsations of sound, as a tone formed by sounding together two notes which are nearly in unison. See ''beat'', ''n.'', 7.—'''7.''' To ponder; be incessantly engaged; be anxiously directed to something; be in agitation or doubt.
{{smaller block|<poem>If you be pleas’d, retire into my cell,
And there repose; a turn or two I’ll walk,
To still my ''beating'' mind.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iv. 1.}}}}
<poem>Thy heaven is on earth; thine eyes and thoughts
''Beat'' on a crown, the treasure of thy heart.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., ii. 1.}}</poem>

'''8.''' ''Naut.'', to make progress against the wind by alternate tacks in a zigzag line. {{smaller|A good square-rigged vessel will make a direct gain to windward of three tenths of the distance she has sailed while beating, while the gain to windward of an average fore-and-aft rigged vessel will be equal to five or six tenths of the distance sailed.}}

{{smaller block|We took a pilot on board, hove up our anchor, and began ''beating'' down the bay.
{{right|''R. H. Dana, Jr.'', Before the Mast, p. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Many yachtsmen had pronounced it to be an impossibility for our vessel to ''beat'' out in so light a breeze.
{{right|''Lady Brassey'', Voyage of Sunbeam, I. i.}}}}

'''To beat about,''' {{smaller|to search by various means or ways; make efforts at discovery.}}

<poem>To find an honest man, I ''beat about.''
{{right|''Pope'', Epil. to Satires, ii. 102.}}</poem>

'''To beat about the bush,''' {{smaller|to approach a matter in a roundabout or circumlocutory way.}}—'''To beat to quarters,''' {{smaller|to summon the crew of a man-of-war by beat of drum to their stations for battle.}}—'''To beat up and down,''' {{smaller|in ''hunting'', to run first one way and then another: said of a stag.}}—'''To beat up for recruits''' {{smaller|or}} '''soldiers,''' {{smaller|to go about to enlist men into the army: a phrase originating in the fact that a recruiting party was often preceded by a drummer with his instrument.}}—'''To beat upon†,''' {{smaller|to enforce by repetition; reiterate.}}

{{smaller block|How frequently and fervently doth the Scripture ''beat upon'' this cause. {{right|''Hakewill.''}}}}

'''beat'''<sup>1</sup> (bēt), ''n.''   [< ''beat''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' A stroke; a striking; a blow, whether with the hand or with a weapon. [Rare.]

<poem>The Smith Divine, as with a careless ''beat'',
Struck out the mute creation at a heat.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Dryden'', Hind and Panther, i. 253.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thus we get but years and ''beats''.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Valentinian, ii. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' A recurrent stroke; a pulsation; a throb: as, the ''beat'' of the pulse; the heart makes from sixty to seventy ''beats'' a minute.—'''3.''' The sound made by the foot in walking or running; a footfall.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''beat'' of her unseen feet,
Which only the angels hear.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', The Cloud.}}}}
'''4.''' A round or course which is frequently gone over: as, a watchman’s ''beat;'' a milkman’s ''beat.''
{{smaller block|We had to descend from the sea-wall, and walk under it, until we got beyond the sentry’s ''beat.''
{{right|''Howells'', Venetian Life, xii.}}}}
Hence—'''5.''' A course habitually traversed, or a place to which one habitually or frequently resorts.—'''6.''' In Alabama and Mississippi, the principal subdivision of a county; a voting-precinct.—'''7.''' In ''music:'' (''a'') The beating or pulsation arising from the interference of two musical notes differing but slightly in pitch. See ''interference.'' {{smaller|The number of beats per second is equal to the difference between the numbers of vibrations of the two notes. Thus, two notes having 256 and 255 vibrations per second respectively, if sounded simultaneously, will give rise to one beat each second, because once in each second the two wave-systems (see ''sound'') will coincide and produce a maximum sound, and once they will be half a wave-length apart, and the sound will almost disappear. Also called ''beating.''}} (''b'') The motion of the hand, foot, or baton in marking the divisions of time during the performance of a piece of music. (''c'') Used vaguely by various English writers to denote different kinds of ornamental notes or graces.—'''8.''' The third operation in paper-making, in which the pulp is still further divided and torn apart in the beating-engine.—'''9.''' The blow struck by a valve when falling into its seat.—'''10.''' The bearing part or the facing of a valve.
{{smaller block|The inlet and outlet valves in the covers of the air-cylinders are of brass provided with leather ''beats.''
{{right|''Ure'', Dict., IV. 740.}}}}
'''11.''' A worthless, dishonest, shiftless fellow; a knave. [Slang.]{{smaller|—'''Beat of a watch''' or '''clock,''' the stroke made by the action of the escapement. A clock is said to be ''in beat'' or ''out of beat'' according as the stroke is at equal or unequal intervals.—'''Beat''' or '''tuck of drum''' (''milit.''), a succession of strokes on a drum, varied in different ways for particular purposes, as to regulate a march, to call soldiers to their arms or quarters, to direct an attack or a retreat, etc.—'''Dead beat.''' (''a'') Formerly, a person without money or resources; now, one who never pays, but lives by evasions; an utterly dishonest, worthless fellow: an intensified expression of ''beat'', 11, above. [Slang.] (''b'') A stroke or blow without recoil, as in the dead-beat escapement. See ''escapement.''—'''Double beat,''' in ''music'', a beat repeated.—'''Out of one’s beat,''' not in one’s sphere or department. [Colloq.]}}

'''beat<sup>1</sup>''' (bēt), ''pp.''   [Shorter form of ''beaten'', which is the only form used attributively.]   Exhausted by exertion, mentally or bodily; fatigued; worn out by toil. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|Quite ''beat'' and very much vexed.
{{right|''Dickens.''}}}}
{{smaller|'''Dead beat,''' completely exhausted or worn out, so as to be incapable of further exertion; utterly baffled, as by the difficulty of a task; thoroughly defeated in a contest or struggle. [Colloq.]}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
